identification.summary: Microsoft's name for an Israel-based private sector offensive actor (PSOA) that sells cyberweapons, mainly malware and zero-day exploits, in hacking-as-a-service packages to government agencies and other malicious actors; Microsoft's current page says the actor was formerly tracked as SOURGUM [S2]. Its main payload is DevilsTongue, a modular, multi-threaded implant written in C and C++ [S1][S2]. Citizen Lab asserted that SOURGUM is the Israeli vendor Candiru; Microsoft's July 2021 blog cited that assertion without itself naming Candiru [S1][S3].
identification.firstObserved: Microsoft publicly disclosed SOURGUM activity and patched two exploited Windows zero-days on 2021-07-13, with its blog published 2021-07-15 [S1]. Earlier activity dates are not stated in the sources gathered.
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Caramel Tsunami (formerly SOURGUM) [S2]. The existing record lists DEV-0236 as a Microsoft in-development designation from Microsoft's mapping file; no fetched or searched source in this pass confirmed that alias, so it is not added. Candiru (also reported as Saito Tech) is a company name, not a Microsoft actor alias; the Candiru-to-Caramel Tsunami link rests on Citizen Lab's assertion cited by Microsoft [S1][S3][S6]. Cluster boundary: ESET's 2021 watering-hole reporting and Avast's 2022 reporting are tied to Candiru by those vendors, not by Microsoft to Caramel Tsunami; keep them separate from Microsoft-observed facts [S5][S6].

attribution.sponsor: Commercial vendor (private sector offensive actor), not a state organization. Microsoft believes SOURGUM is Israel-based and says buyers include government agencies [S1][S2].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states it believes the actor is Israel-based [S1]. Citizen Lab asserted that SOURGUM is Candiru; Microsoft's 2021 blog cites that assertion without itself naming Candiru [S1]. The 'high confidence' wording was not verifiable in this pass. ESET said it thought a Candiru client carried out the 2021 watering-hole attacks it observed, and did not name the client [S5].
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry and malware analysis of DevilsTongue and two Windows zero-days [S1]; Citizen Lab analysis of a sample shared by Microsoft and of related infrastructure [S1][S3]; ESET and Avast links to Candiru-associated tooling [S5][S6]. US Commerce Department listed Candiru on the Entity List on 2021-11-03 for supplying spyware to foreign governments, as reported by Baker McKenzie [S4].

objectives: Revenue from selling intrusion tools and access to government customers and other buyers [S2]. Victim selection appears to reflect customer interests: Microsoft identified more than 100 victims including politicians, human rights activists, journalists, academics, embassy workers and political dissidents [S1]. Microsoft notes victim location does not necessarily indicate the customer's country [S1].

regions: Palestinian Authority (about half of identified victims) [S1]
Israel, Iran, Lebanon, Yemen, Spain (Catalonia), United Kingdom, Turkey, Armenia, Singapore [S1]
Yemen-focused watering holes plus Iran, Syria, Saudi Arabia, UK media (ESET, Candiru-linked, not Microsoft-attributed) [S5]
targeting.notes: Microsoft victim data covers the 2021 disclosure [S1]. Regional detail from ESET and Avast concerns activity those vendors tied to Candiru and is not Microsoft's attribution to Caramel Tsunami [S5][S6].

capabilities.summary: Delivery of browser exploits, including zero-days, via single-use URLs sent through messaging apps such as WhatsApp, followed by two Windows zero-day privilege escalations (CVE-2021-31979 integer overflow in the kernel and CVE-2021-33771 race condition use-after-free) for sandbox escape and kernel code execution; both were fixed in July 2021 updates [S1][S2]. DevilsTongue is modular and multi-threaded with user-mode and kernel-mode components, persists via COM hijacking running in svchost.exe as SYSTEM, steals credentials from LSASS and browsers, decrypts and exfiltrates Signal conversations, steals browser cookies to access and send messages from victim web accounts, and uses the signed driver physmem.sys to proxy API calls through the kernel [S1]. Avast reported a Candiru-linked Chrome zero-day (CVE-2022-2294, WebRTC heap overflow) in 2022 watering-hole attacks [S6].

campaigns.name: SOURGUM / DevilsTongue disclosure
campaigns.summary: Microsoft and Citizen Lab publicly describe more than 100 victims, two exploited Windows zero-days (CVE-2021-31979, CVE-2021-33771) patched 2021-07-13, and DevilsTongue spyware; Citizen Lab asserts the actor is Candiru [S1][S3].

campaigns.name: US Entity List designation of Candiru
campaigns.summary: Commerce Department added Candiru, NSO Group and two other entities to the Entity List, with law-firm sources giving the final rule date as 2021-11-03 (BIS press release dated 2021-11-04), citing supply of spyware to foreign governments, per Baker McKenzie coverage [S4].

campaigns.name: ESET watering-hole reporting (Candiru-linked)
campaigns.summary: ESET reported watering-hole attacks on Middle East websites, focused on Yemen, and said a Candiru client likely carried them out; it could not recover an exploit or final payload and saw no activity after end of July 2021. Attribution to Candiru is ESET's, not Microsoft's [S5].

campaigns.name: Avast report of Candiru Chrome zero-day (CVE-2022-2294)
campaigns.summary: Avast linked a Chrome WebRTC zero-day, fixed by Google on 2022-07-04, to Candiru watering-hole attacks mostly against Lebanon, with targets also in Turkey, Yemen and Palestine after a March 2022 toolset revamp, per The Hacker News coverage. Attribution is Avast's [S6].

campaigns.name: Microsoft renames SOURGUM as Caramel Tsunami
campaigns.summary: Microsoft's Security Insider page, dated 2024-01-25, presents the actor as Caramel Tsunami, formerly SOURGUM [S2].

diamond.adversary: Israel-based commercial vendor selling intrusion tools to governments and other buyers; Citizen Lab asserts it is Candiru [S1][S2][S3].
diamond.capability: Browser and Windows zero-day exploit chain, DevilsTongue modular spyware, COM-hijack persistence, signed-driver abuse (physmem.sys), Signal and cookie theft [S1].
diamond.infrastructure: Single-use URLs delivered via messaging apps; Microsoft listed multiple malicious domains and host indicators such as physmem.sys in system32\drivers and hijack DLLs under system32\ime [S1]. Citizen Lab reported hundreds of related domains, which could not be verified from the fetched pages [S3].
diamond.victim: Politicians, activists, journalists, academics, embassy staff and dissidents, roughly half in the Palestinian Authority [S1].
diamond.socioPolitical: Commercial surveillance market serving government customers; Commerce Department Entity List action in November 2021 reflects US policy concern over spyware use against officials, journalists and activists [S2][S4].
diamond.technology: Unpatched Windows kernel and browser flaws, links opened from messaging apps, Windows hosts without Credential Guard or vulnerable-driver blocking [S1].

gaps: DEV-0236 alias is listed in Microsoft's mapping file used by this record, but no source found in this pass confirms it for Caramel Tsunami.

Microsoft's 2021 blog does not itself name Candiru; only Citizen Lab's assertion is cited [S1]. A search summary of a Microsoft slide deck on Caramel Tsunami suggests Microsoft later linked the actor to Candiru; that deck is not cited and was not opened.

Primary documents not opened: Citizen Lab 'Hooking Candiru', Commerce Federal Register rule, ESET and Avast original reports (hosts unreachable from fetch; relied on search summaries or secondary coverage).

No public Microsoft reporting found on Caramel Tsunami activity after 2021; current operations, customers and ownership changes are unverified. A reported 2025 acquisition of Candiru appeared only on Wikipedia and is not used.
Exploits for the ESET 2021 and Avast 2022 incidents were not fully recovered; links to Microsoft's cluster rest on Candiru attribution by those vendors.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1: Key terrain is personal and corporate endpoints of high-value individuals (officials, embassy staff, journalists, dissidents), their messaging apps and browsers, and websites they frequent [S1][S5]. STEP 2: The actor is a vendor, so capability (zero-day chains, kernel-level implant) is high but targeting is set by customers; sponsor intent cannot be inferred from the vendor alone [S1][S2]. STEP 3: Observed template is single-use link via messaging app or watering-hole site, browser exploit, Windows kernel privilege escalation, DevilsTongue implant, then credential, Signal and cookie theft [S1][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is continued customer-driven surveillance of civil-society and political targets in the Middle East and nearby regions. MDCOA is use of a vendor zero-day chain against government or military personnel or their families through personal messaging apps. Candidate indicators: physmem.sys at system32\drivers, DLLs beginning 'im.' under system32\ime, .dat files under system32\config subfolders, WimBootConfigurations.ini, and Microsoft-listed domains [S1].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. (1) Situational awareness: track out-of-band browser and Windows zero-day advisories, since this vendor chains both [S1][S6]. (2) Authorities: personal devices and messaging apps of personnel fall outside many network defense authorities; coordinate with counterintelligence and force protection for travel and high-risk personnel guidance. (3) Mission assurance: Credential Guard, vulnerable-driver blocking rules and isolated browsing for untrusted links are Microsoft-recommended mitigations [S1]. (4) Coordination: share indicators with DC3 and partners, and note that vendor-supplied tools can appear against allied or coalition personnel regardless of the buyer's identity [S1][S4].
